title: By night, from mosque to mosque
hookLine: glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque (17:1)

cards: Surah seventeen opens with a whole night, and tells it in a single verse. No buildup, no description of the road. Just a sentence of praise, and inside it, a journey.

The surah is named for that night: Al-Isra, the Night Journey. Its other name is Bani Isra'il, the Children of Israel. Some Muslims mark the night each year in the month of Rajab, though its date is debated.

teach.h: SUBHANA: GLORY TO THE ONE WHO CARRIED.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship".
The verse goes on: whose surroundings We have blessed, so that We might show him some of Our signs. Start with the first word, subhana: glory be, far above any fault.
The verse opens with praise of the One who did the carrying, not the one who was carried. And notice what he's called. Not prophet, not messenger. 'Abd: servant.
On that night, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is named by a humble title. Then the two places. The Sacred Mosque is in Mecca, around the Ka'bah.
The Farthest Mosque, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, is understood by Muslims as Jerusalem. Masjid literally means a place of prostration. The hadith collections fill in what the verse leaves out.

teach.h: MECCA TO JERUSALEM, THEN THE ASCENT.
teach.b: In Bukhari and Muslim, a white mount named Buraq carries him; in Muslim's collection he leads the earlier prophets in prayer in Jerusalem; then comes the Mi'raj, the ascent through the heavens, where the five daily prayers are given.
Scholars have discussed the nature of the journey from early on. Commentators such as at-Tabari held it was in body and spirit; some early reports describe it as a vision.

teach.h: AFTER A YEAR OF LOSS, SOME SAY.
teach.b: Some biographies place it in a hard season, after the Prophet had lost his wife Khadijah and his uncle Abu Talib, when doors in Mecca and Ta'if were closing; its date is debated.
Read that way, the night comes in the middle of loss: not carried away from trouble, but shown signs in the middle of it.

how: Some Muslims mark Laylat al-Isra wal-Mi'raj, commonly on 27 Rajab, with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and talks retelling the journey; practice varies, and some scholars caution against fixing special rites to the date.

o: the night the Qur'an was first sent down to the Prophet
the Isra, a servant carried in the dark to see signs
a vigil of prayer kept until dawn in Ramadan

games.q: inside the night journey — tap the pairs.
p: glory be, far above any fault
the ascent; the five prayers given

s: 17:1 calls him prophet in describing the journey
masjid literally means a place of prostration
a place where people bow down.
the verse itself describes Buraq and the ascent
the verse is one sentence; Buraq and the Mi'raj come from the hadith collections.

games.q: you've lost your wife and your uncle in the same season, and doors are closing around you. what does the night bring, as some biographies tell it?
o: a sign that it's time to give up.
a journey by night, and signs shown to him.
an easy year with no more trouble.
games.why: he is carried by night from Mecca to Jerusalem and shown signs, in the middle of a hard season, as those biographies tell it, not after it.

practice: Look at the night sky if it's dark, or through a window, or close your eyes and remember the last clear night you saw, and notice how far away the farthest light is. Let yourself feel small under it, not in a bad way.
If you pray, say subhan Allah, glory to God, once, quietly.

wordCard.voice: By night. The Isra: a servant carried from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, in the dark, to be shown signs. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: He carried His servant by night (17:1). Isra, the night journey, comes from this verb.

carryVoice: Your line: taken by night. Some signs only show up in the dark. Until tomorrow.
